summary: Explains how SIP Back-to-Back User Agents that sit on the media path should handle STUN messages. Since a B2BUA bridges separate media legs, it must treat STUN connectivity checks correctly.

eli5.summary: A middleman who relays calls must also pass connection-test pings in the right way.

questions: stun messages in back-to-back user agents
how does a b2bua handle ice
what is ice termination in sip
subtitle: How a SIP middlebox on the media path should treat ICE and STUN, so calls through it still connect and stay secure.

tldr.problem: SIP Back-to-Back User Agents (B2BUAs) often sit on the media path and rewrite SDP. Without clear rules they break ICE, either by hiding it from the endpoints or by triggering an ice-mismatch that aborts ICE processing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines what a B2BUA MUST do with ICE in SDP and with STUN packets. It either terminates ICE on each leg with fresh credentials and its own candidates, or passes the endpoints' candidates and credentials through and adds its own.
tldr.outcome: A B2BUA that follows these rules keeps ICE working across its legs. The RFC also requires the signaling channel to be encrypted so the STUN short-term key stays secret.

today: RFC 7584 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2015, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines B2BUA behavior for ICE and STUN handling, building on RFC 5245.

sections.title: Why B2BUAs Need STUN and ICE Rules
sections.content:
Many SIP deployments put entities on the signaling and media path that go beyond a traditional SIP proxy. These B2BUAs (Back-to-Back User Agents, described in RFC 7092) often use proprietary mechanisms to help SIP devices behind NATs communicate. SIP and SDP carry IP addresses and ports that are unreachable when peers are separated by NATs, which is the problem STUN, TURN and ICE were later built to solve.

Hosted NAT Traversal as described in RFC 7362 has weaknesses. Its common 'restricted-latching' approach can be attacked by someone who can see the source address of the SIP user agent. ICE adds authentication tokens in the ice-ufrag and ice-pwd attributes, so a peer's identity can be confirmed before media flows.

The trouble starts when a B2BUA modifies SDP. Some remove all ICE attributes, so the endpoints think the other side lacks ICE. Others pass the ICE attributes unchanged but rewrite the m= and c= lines, which is detected as an ice-mismatch and ICE processing is aborted. This RFC defines consistent behavior to avoid both outcomes.
sections.eli5: Imagine a receptionist passing notes between two people who want to meet. If the receptionist scribbles over the meeting details, the two get confused. This RFC says how to pass the notes properly.

sections.title: Signaling-only B2BUAs
sections.content:
The RFC sorts B2BUAs by how deeply they touch the media. The simplest case is an SDP-Modifying Signaling-only B2BUA: it is not on the media path, but it does edit SDP bodies. Such a B2BUA MUST NOT change the IP address in the c= line, the port in the m= line, or the ICE semantics of the SDP, because doing so can cause an ice-mismatch.

B2BUAs that operate on the media plane fall into three categories taken from RFC 7092: a simple media relay that only changes the transport header, a media-aware B2BUA that inspects or changes RTP or RTCP headers but not payload, and a media-termination B2BUA, such as a transcoder, that works on the payload. All three MUST follow the media-plane behavior in the sections below.
sections.eli5: If the middleman only passes notes along, it must not change the meeting place written on them. If it also carries the packages, it needs the longer set of rules.

sections.title: Media Plane B2BUAs: Overview
sections.content:
When one or both endpoints are behind a NAT and a B2BUA sits between them, the B2BUA MUST support ICE, or at a minimum ICE lite as described in RFC 5245. It MUST also use the mechanism in Section 2.2 of RFC 5245 to separate STUN packets from media packets arriving on the RTP/RTCP port.

There are two modes. In mandatory ICE termination the B2BUA wants to stay on the media path, for example for address hiding or for interworking between ICE and non-ICE endpoints. It ends ICE on each side, so it has two ICE contexts. In optional ICE termination the B2BUA only wants to be on the path to help with NAT traversal. It passes candidates and STUN short-term credentials across after adding its own candidates.
sections.eli5: The middleman can either always stand between the two people, or only step in if they cannot find each other directly.

sections.title: Mandatory ICE Termination
sections.content:
A B2BUA that always wants to be on the media path follows these rules when it sends out SDP:

  • It MUST advertise ICE support and MAY include its own candidates of different types for each component of each media stream.
  • In ICE lite mode it MUST send an a=ice-lite attribute and MUST include its host candidates for each component of each media stream.
  • It MUST generate new ice-ufrag and ice-pwd values and MUST NOT propagate the ones it received, so the credentials differ on the two legs.
  • It MUST NOT pass on the incoming candidate list, advertising only its own, and it MUST put its default candidate in the c= and m= lines. That keeps it on the media path.

The B2BUA terminates ICE messages on each leg and does not propagate them. Connectivity checks on the two legs run in parallel as two independent ICE contexts, using ICE lite or full ICE procedures from RFC 5245. Because the contexts are independent, checks can finish on one side before the other. Media that arrives meanwhile is sent to the other side on the default candidate address from the c= line.
sections.eli5: The middleman writes brand new secret passwords for each side and gives only its own address. Each person then talks only to the middleman, who relays everything.

sections.title: Optional ICE Termination
sections.content:
A B2BUA that wants to be on the media path only for NAT traversal does something different. It copies the candidate list from the incoming SDP, appends its own candidates, and copies the received ufrag and password values to the outgoing SDP.

Its own candidates MAY have lower priority than the endpoints' candidates. The endpoints' own pairs are then tested first, and the B2BUA is used only if all the candidate pairs formed between the two endpoints fail. After the offer/answer exchange the endpoints use the ICE procedures in Section 8 of RFC 5245 to nominate a pair for media.

In the RFC's example, the B2BUA leaves the default candidate in the c= and m= lines as the endpoint sent it. If the B2BUA wants to be on the path when ICE between the endpoints fails, or when one endpoint lacks ICE, it overwrites those lines with its own address and port.
sections.eli5: The middleman adds its own address to the list but lets the two people try each other first. It only steps in if they cannot connect directly.

sections.title: Forked Signaling
sections.content: Forking can cause a B2BUA to receive several answers to a single outbound INVITE. In that case the B2BUA SHOULD apply the termination procedures described for the single-answer case to every answer it receives. The RFC gives no further detail on forking.
sections.eli5: If several people answer the same call, the middleman handles each answer using the same rules as before.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ICE uses the STUN short-term credential mechanism for authentication and message integrity. STUN connectivity checks carry a MESSAGE-INTEGRITY attribute holding an HMAC-SHA1 of the STUN message, computed with a key exchanged in the signaling channel.

For that reason the signaling channel between the endpoints and the B2BUA MUST be encrypted. Otherwise eavesdroppers could see the key, and the security benefit of short-term authentication would be lost.
sections.eli5: The passwords are passed in the note, so the note must be sealed. If anyone can read it, the passwords protect nothing.
